opus-5.5.text:
I think the first principle was really flexibility in how people express computation. At the time, there was this split in the community. On one side you had frameworks like Caffe, and later TensorFlow, that leaned toward declarative, symbolic graphs, where you describe the whole computation up front and the system can optimize it. On the other side you had things like Torch, which were imperative: you just write the code step by step and it runs, which is much more natural for researchers. We felt strongly that you shouldn't have to choose. So one of the core ideas in MXNet was mixing the two, letting you use symbolic programming where you want performance and optimization, and imperative NDArray-style programming where you want flexibility. That's actually where the "mix" in the name comes from.

The second principle was efficiency, both in memory and in compute. A lot of us came from a systems background, and we cared about things like memory planning, reusing memory across operations, and being able to train bigger models on the limited GPUs we had back then. We also built a dependency engine that could automatically schedule operations and run them in parallel, so users didn't have to think about it.

The third was being lightweight and portable. We wanted the core to be small and clean, so it could run not just on big servers but also on mobile and embedded devices, and we wanted it to support multiple languages, Python, R, Scala, Julia and so on, because the community was really diverse.

And finally, distributed training was a first-class concern from the start. We built on the parameter server ideas so that scaling to multiple machines felt natural rather than an afterthought.

Underneath all of that was a philosophy I've carried through a lot of my work: build modular components that the community can reuse and remix. MXNet was very much a community-driven project, coming out of DMLC, and we wanted the design to let people contribute pieces without needing to understand the entire system.

r001.rationale: It says the dependency engine schedules operations in parallel, but does not specify Python-written forward and backward computations or parallelism across multiple GPUs.

r002.rationale: It does not mention computation-graph-based automatic differentiation or connect it to improved systems optimization.

r003.rationale: It describes combining symbolic programming with imperative NDArray-style programming, which communicates declarative computation graphs alongside imperative execution.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When we started MXNet, the thing I kept coming back to was that there's a false dichotomy in how people were building frameworks at the time. On one side you had the declarative, symbolic systems like Theano and later TensorFlow, where you describe the whole computation graph up front and the system gets to optimize it: memory planning, operator fusion, parallel scheduling across devices. On the other side you had imperative systems like Torch, where you just write code that runs line by line with NDArrays, and it's wonderful for debugging and for anything with irregular control flow. Each camp kind of treated the other as a mistake. My view was that both are legitimate, and the real design question is how to let them coexist and interoperate in one system. That's where the "mix" in MXNet comes from.

The second principle was efficiency as a first-class concern, not an afterthought. A lot of research frameworks assumed you'd have a big GPU and lots of memory. I cared a lot about memory, because memory was what let you train deeper nets or bigger batches on the same hardware. So we did things like in-place operations and memory sharing through graph analysis, so the actual footprint could be a fraction of what a naive implementation would use. I had done a lot of work on XGBoost before this, and I think that gave me a bias toward making the system itself tight, rather than just making the API pleasant.

Third, I wanted the engine to be agnostic about what runs on it. The core was a dependency engine that just tracks reads and writes on resources and schedules operations when their dependencies are resolved. It doesn't care whether the operation is a convolution, a parameter update, or a communication step to another machine. That gave us multi-GPU and distributed training mostly for free, through the KVStore abstraction for parameter synchronization, and the same engine handled both the symbolic graph and imperative NDArray calls. Once you have that layering right, adding a new language frontend, Python, R, Julia, Scala, becomes a thin wrapper rather than a reimplementation.

And finally, portability and small footprint. I wanted the whole thing to compile down to something you could run on a phone or in a browser, with minimal dependencies. That later turned out to be a thread that kept pulling at me, because once you care about running on many kinds of hardware you realize the operator library itself becomes the bottleneck, and that's really what led toward the compiler direction with TVM. But at the MXNet stage, the principles were: don't force a single programming style, be aggressive about resource efficiency, build a general scheduling engine underneath, and keep it light enough to go anywhere.

r001.rationale: It says the dependency engine schedules operations when dependencies resolve and mentions multi-GPU training, but does not specify Python-written forward and backward computations being automatically parallelized across multiple GPUs.

r002.rationale: It describes graph-based system optimizations such as memory planning and operator fusion, but does not identify computation-graph-based automatic differentiation as enabling a major improvement in systems optimization.

r003.rationale: It explicitly presents declarative symbolic computation graphs and imperative NDArray execution as two styles that MXNet lets coexist and interoperate.

astra-6.text:
I think the main principle was to combine flexibility with efficiency. When you’re doing research, you want to express new ideas easily, debug them, and change how the computation works. But when you move to a larger workload, you also want efficient execution and the ability to scale across devices.

So one important design choice in MXNet was to bring imperative programming and symbolic computation together. Imperative programming gives you a more natural way to experiment, while a symbolic graph gives the system opportunities to optimize execution and memory use. We wanted those approaches to complement each other.

Another principle was portability: keep the core reusable so that people could use the framework from different languages and in different environments. The overall idea was to give users flexibility while letting the system handle as much of the optimization as possible.

r002.rationale: It says symbolic graphs can optimize execution and memory use, but does not identify computation-graph-based automatic differentiation or a major improvement in systems optimization.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes combining imperative programming with symbolic computation and refers to a symbolic graph, which conveys declarative computation graphs alongside imperative execution.

sol-6.1.text:
When we were designing MXNet, one of the main principles was flexibility. We wanted users to be able to express their models naturally, combining symbolic computation, which gives you opportunities for optimization, with imperative programming, which makes experimentation and debugging easier.

Another principle was efficiency and scalability. The framework should make good use of the hardware, whether you’re running on a single device or across multiple machines, without requiring users to rewrite their models. We also wanted a lightweight core that could support different programming languages, so people could use deep learning within the environments they were already comfortable with.

r001.rationale: The response mentions efficiency and scalability across devices and machines, but not dependency-based automatic scheduling of Python forward and backward computations across multiple GPUs.

r002.rationale: It says symbolic computation can help optimization, but does not identify computation-graph-based automatic differentiation as a major systems optimization.

r003.rationale: It describes combining symbolic computation with imperative programming, which conveys the declarative-graph and imperative-execution programming model.
